topic: Functions of RBI and Monetary Policy
description: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the central bank of India. It formulates, implements, and monitors the monetary policy to maintain price stability while keeping in mind the objective of economic growth.

sections.title: History and Establishment of RBI
sections.description: Important historical milestones related to the foundation, framework, and early years of the Reserve Bank of India.

historical_events.significance: The Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance recommended the establishment of a central bank in India.
The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 was passed, which provided the statutory framework for the functioning of the bank.
The RBI commenced its operations as a private shareholders' bank with an initial share capital of Rs. 5 Crores.
Post-independence, the RBI was nationalised and became fully owned by the Government of India.

important_facts.fact: The first Governor of the RBI was Sir Osborne Smith, while the first Indian Governor was C. D. Deshmukh.
The initial headquarters of the RBI was in Calcutta, but it was permanently moved to Mumbai in 1937.

sections.title: Major Functions of RBI
sections.description: The primary roles and responsibilities performed by the RBI as the apex central banking institution.

key_concepts.explanation: RBI has the sole right to issue all bank notes except One Rupee notes and coins, which are issued by the Ministry of Finance.
It manages the accounts of Central and State Governments, provides them with banking services, and gives short-term loans called Ways and Means Advances (WMA).
It acts as the Lender of Last Resort for commercial banks, provides them with financial assistance in times of need, and holds their cash reserves.
It manages India's foreign exchange reserves and maintains the external value of the Rupee under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999.

sections.title: Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)
sections.description: The statutory body responsible for determining the policy interest rates required to achieve the inflation target in India.

key_concepts.explanation: Constituted in 2016 on the recommendation of the Urjit Patel Committee, it is a 6-member body (3 from RBI and 3 appointed by the Government of India).
The MPC is mandated to maintain Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation at 4% with a tolerance band of ±2% (i.e., between 2% and 6%).

important_facts.fact: The Governor of the Reserve Bank of India acts as the ex-officio Chairman of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC).

sections.title: Quantitative Tools of Monetary Policy
sections.description: Instruments used by the RBI to regulate the overall volume of money supply and liquidity in the economy.

key_concepts.explanation: The interest rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against approved government securities.
The interest rate at which the RBI borrows funds from commercial banks for the short term, used to absorb excess liquidity from the market.
The minimum percentage of a bank's Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that it must maintain as cash balances with the RBI.
The percentage of NDTL that banks must maintain with themselves in the form of liquid assets like cash, gold, or approved government securities.
The buying and selling of government securities in the open market by the RBI to inject or absorb liquidity in the economy.
A penal rate at which scheduled banks can borrow overnight funds from the RBI by dipping into their SLR quota in emergency situations.

sections.title: Qualitative Tools of Monetary Policy
sections.description: Selective instruments used by the RBI to regulate the direction of credit flow to specific sectors of the economy.

key_concepts.explanation: The difference between the loan amount granted by the bank and the market value of the collateral pledged by the borrower.
An informal mechanism where the RBI requests and persuades commercial banks to follow its directives and monetary policy guidelines.
Punitive measures, such as imposing fines or canceling licenses, taken by the RBI against banks that continuously violate its rules and regulations.
